Where it began

Aakash Chopra was born in Agra on 19 September 1977 and studied at Hindu College in the University of Delhi. His cricket grew up with Delhi, the side he played for over many seasons, and one of his team-mates there was Virender Sehwag. When India went looking for someone to open with Sehwag in Tests, they turned to Chopra.

The player

His Test debut came against New Zealand at Ahmedabad in late 2003, and in the next match, at Mohali, he made two fifties. That winter in Australia he and Sehwag put on two hundred stands for the first wicket, at Melbourne and at Sydney, and his steady starts were given much of the credit for the big totals India ran up behind them, even with Tendulkar, Dravid, Ganguly and Laxman waiting to follow.

He was at the other end in Multan when Sehwag made India's first Test triple hundred, and he made 42 himself. His Test career was a brief one: 10 matches across 2003 and 2004, with 437 runs at 23.00, a best of 60, and 15 catches.

What made him special

Patience. He was content to bat time at the top, and the great batsmen behind him made the most of the starts he gave them. Domestic cricket gave him the longer run he deserved: he made more than 8,000 first-class runs and won the Ranji Trophy three times, once with Delhi and twice with Rajasthan, helping them become the first Plate division side to lift it.

Nobody ever confused him with a Twenty20 slogger. Two seasons with the Kolkata Knight Riders brought him 53 runs; his gifts were made for the longer game.

Away from the middle

After retiring from all cricket in 2015 he became a familiar voice on the game. He commentated for Star Sports over many years, worked on the 2018–19 series in Australia, moved into Hindi commentary, and was on the Hindi panel for the 2025 Champions Trophy. In 2020 he became the first commentator to voice a mobile cricket game.

He has also written widely. His first book, Beyond the Blues, a diary of the 2007–2008 domestic season, came out in 2009 and was warmly praised. Out of the Blue, about Rajasthan's Ranji title, followed in 2011, then The Insider in 2015 and Numbers Do Lie in 2017. He also took to YouTube, with a channel of match previews and reviews.

And finally

His commentary is known for its one-liners and rhymes. For an opener who liked to take his time over his runs, he has never been short of words.
